title: Benchmarking Weighted A* across Obstacle Densities and Heuristic Weights
description: Define run_trial to run astar_weighted on a 28x40 grid and sweep obstacle probability p in [0.15, 0.22, 0.30] and heuristic weight w in [1.0, 1.2, 1.5].
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Define `run_trial(W=40, H=28, p=0.22, w=1.0, seed=0)` to create a `(H, W)` obstacle grid with density `p`. Run `astar_weighted` with `weight=w` and `h_m(c) = manhattan(c, goal)`, and return `(solved, path_len, expanded, time_sec)`.
Use nested loops over `p in [0.15, 0.22, 0.30]` and `w in [1.0, 1.2, 1.5]` to run `run_trial(p=p, w=w, seed=42)` and print `solved`, `path_len`, `expanded`, and elapsed time in milliseconds.
Look at lines 7-9 and 12-13: for each fixed obstacle density `p`, `seed=42` gives the exact same grid. The inner loop tests `w = 1.0` (standard A*), `w = 1.2`, and `w = 1.5` (weighted A*).

steps.question: How many total calls to `run_trial` do the nested loops on lines 12-14 make? Why does passing the same `seed=42` on line 14 matter when comparing `w = 1.0, 1.2, 1.5`?
steps.answer: The two 3-element loops make `3 * 3 = 9` calls to `run_trial`. Fixing `seed=42` guarantees that for a given `p`, all three heuristic weights `w` are evaluated on the exact same obstacle layout.

steps.description: On the first iteration (`p = 0.15`, `w = 1.0`), line 14 calls `run_trial(p=0.15, w=1.0, seed=42)`.
Inside `run_trial`, line 7 invokes `astar_weighted` on the `28 x 40` grid from `(1, 1)` to `(26, 37)`.
